title: Labor’s home support scheme panned
full_text:
State governments have slammed federal Labor’s new aged care home support scheme, with the West Australian ALP saying the assessment algorithm was so inflexible that it left an Alzheimer’s patient and their 92-year-old carer waiting up to nine months for service to start.
WA Aged Care Minister Simone McGurk said the new scheme “has not lived up to its promise” and that the 7500-long queue in her state to access aged care home services was “unacceptable”.
The Albanese government is changing the way aged care support at home programs are administered and assessed but the rollout so far has been bumpy.
Labor was forced to extend the life of the old system because it resulted in a massive jump in waiting lists and there were reports of elderly Australians dying while waiting for aid for which they had been already approved.
With the new program now under way, state governments have now said the scheme still is not working as intended.
The Tasmanian Liberal government and Queensland Liberal National government railed against the fact the commonwealth had announced ending the extra rebate for private health insurance for Australians aged over 65, saying that decision would make the aged care crisis even worse.
This goes to the heart of the Labor government’s justification for the decision, given it has been saying that it was a “difficult” budget decision but that it needed to find more money for more aged care beds.
“This policy may have unintended consequences for older Australians who rely on private health cover for more timely access to services,” the Queensland Health Department wrote in a submission to the Support at Home program Senate inquiry. “If more older Australians rely solely on public health services, hospitals are likely to see increased demand for elective surgeries, emergency care, and inpatient services.
“This could exacerbate waiting lists, increase strain on hospital staff, and reduce system capacity to respond to both routine and urgent care needs.” Tasmania said it was “concerned about the removal of higher private health insurance rebates for older Australians”.
“Higher premiums may lead older Australians to drop or reduce their cover, which may increase their reliance on the public health system and place additional pressure on hospitals,” its submission read.
Those two states – along with Labor-led NSW – have already come out publicly against the federal government plan to abolish higher private health insurance for over-65-year-olds.
The WA Labor government was scathing of the way federal Labor’s Support at Home program had played out. “The state government has long supported the policy intent of the commonwealth’s aged care reforms, including the commencement of the Support at Home program in November 2025,” Ms McGurk wrote.
“I remain hopeful that Support at Home will allow more older people to choose to live at home safely and with dignity for as long as possible. However, to date the program has not lived up to its promise for many older people and families.” Ms McGurk said “there are still around 7500 older Western Australians waiting for Support at Home – this is unacceptable”.
“Additionally, wait times from assessment to service commencement are unreasonably long.” She said the transition between the two schemes had left many constituents telling her they were worse off, and urged a “local override” for assessments for home care packages under the scheme.
“The current criteria mechanism is not responsive to complex and nuanced circumstances and assessors need flexibility to address immediate individual needs,” Ms McGurk said.
When contacted for comment, a government spokesman said the Albanese government had “spent four years repairing the mess the Coalition left behind” and acknowledged “there’s more to do”. “We’re bringing down wait times for home care and it’s having a material impact for older people,” he said. “We’ll continue to invest to meet the challenge of unprecedented demand and make sure older Australians get the care they need sooner.”
